paragraphs.heading: A column of old snow
paragraphs.text: An ice core is a long cylinder of ice drilled out of an ice sheet or a high mountain glacier. Snow piles up layer by layer each year, so the deeper ice is older and a single core spans many years. Shallow cores can be taken with hand augers, while powered drills can go down more than two miles (3.2 km) and bring up ice as old as 800,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: From snow to sealed air
paragraphs.text: As snow builds up, each layer presses on those beneath it until they become denser and turn into firn, which is still not dense enough to stop air escaping. At a density of about 830 kg/m³ the firn becomes ice, and the air inside is shut into bubbles that hold a sample of the atmosphere from when the ice formed. In Greenland and Antarctica this happens between 64 m and 115 m down. At Summit Camp in Greenland it happens at 77 m, and that ice is 230 years old; the Antarctic site Dome C gives 95 m and 2500 years. Near 1500 m the ice crystals change from hexagonal to cubic and the air moves into them, so the bubbles vanish and the ice turns clearer. Two or three feet of snow can end up as less than a foot of ice.

paragraphs.heading: What the ice records
paragraphs.text: The ice and the material trapped in it can be used to rebuild the climate over the whole age of a core. The proportions of different oxygen and hydrogen isotopes give clues to past temperatures, and the trapped air shows the levels of gases such as carbon dioxide. Because heat moves very slowly through a big ice sheet, the temperature down the borehole is another clue to past temperature. Specks in the ice tell about conditions when they settled: soot and ash from forest fires and volcanoes, beryllium-10 made by cosmic rays, micrometeorites and pollen. All these lines of data can be put together to pick out whichever climate model fits them best.

paragraphs.heading: Dust, salt and time stamps
paragraphs.text: What gets trapped can depend on where the ice formed. Cores near coasts are more likely to hold material from the sea, such as sea salt ions. Greenland cores contain layers of wind-blown dust that match cold, dry periods, when wind scoured cold deserts. Radioactive elements, whether natural or from nuclear weapons tests, help date the layers. Volcanic eruptions strong enough to spread material around the globe left marks in many cores, which lets scientists line up the timelines of different cores.

paragraphs.heading: Light and dark bands
paragraphs.text: Cores are often drilled in Antarctica and central Greenland, where it is almost never warm enough to melt, yet summer sunlight still alters the snow. Near the poles the Sun stays up day and night in summer and stays out of sight all winter. The summer Sun can cause some snow to sublimate, so the top inch or so ends up less dense. As the Sun nears its lowest point, it gets colder and hoar frost forms on top; once buried, this coarse frost packs into lighter layers than the winter snow. The result is alternating bands of lighter and darker ice in the core.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing where to drill
paragraphs.text: The weight of ice above makes the deep layers thin and flow outward, and that flow can distort the layers. So it is best to drill deep cores where the ice barely flows, and such places can be found with maps of the flow lines. Scientists have been studying ice cores since the early 20th century. Decades of Soviet drilling at Vostok Station in Antarctica produced a core reaching 3769 m.
